newsitem.title: USA: US CORPORATE BONDS- Primary sector takes spotlight.
newsitem.headline: US CORPORATE BONDS- Primary sector takes spotlight.

text.p: The primary sector stole the corporate bond spotlight on Monday as issuers brought $1.2 billion in new supply, in sharp contrast to a dull trading session on the secondary front, players said.
"Most of Monday's activity in the high-grade sector revolved around new issues," said one trader. "Secondary trading was extremely light."

Issuance in the investment-grade arena was boosted as interest rates continued to fall, creating an attractive window of opportunity for U.S. corporations looking to finance debt at cheaper levels, syndicate players said.
Currently, the 10-year U.S. Treasury note is trading up 11/32 at 102-21/32 to yield 6.26 percent. The benchmark 30-year bond is up 20/32 at 100-20/32 to yield 6.58 percent.
Among Monday's opportunistic issuers was American International Group unit, International Lease Finance Co, with $100 million in A1/A-plus four-year notes at 34.5 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.
Another $250 million came from Anheuser-Busch Cos Inc, which sold $250 million in A1/A-plus rated 20-year debentures at 63 basis points over Treasuries.
Also, Federal Express capitalized on shorter long-term rates to issue $250 million in Baa2/BBB rated 100-year bonds at 103 basis points over Treasuries.

Another $600 million in debt was brought by Commercial Credit Co via a A1/A-plus rated two-part debt offering. The deal included $300 million in five-year notes at 32.4 basis points and $300 million in 10-year notes 54 basis points over.

In other news, Northrop Grumman Corp debt tightened another three basis points for a total of 18 basis points since news of its merger with aerospace giant, Lockheed Martin Corp last Thursday, traders said.
"Before news of the merger, Northrop's debt was quoted 75 basis points bid, with no offer," said one high-grade trader. "Since then the bonds have tightened substantially."
The defense contractor's 7.0 percent paper due 2006 was bid 57 basis points, narrowing further from Thursday's closing level of 60 basis points bid, traders said.
Northrop's 7-7/8 percent paper was 78 bid, 70 offer, traders said this issue was 20 basis points tighter since the news.
Players said no change was seen in Lockheed Martin's debt since the news hit the street.
Turning to the high-yield sector, Payless Cashways 9-1/8 percent paper due 2003 continued its decline, falling another three points to a 24 bid, 24-1/2 offer, traders said.
Players said the specialty retailer of building materials has seen a steady decline in its bonds since last month.
"It seems like its been a quick trip to the 20's ... the bonds were trading at a 32 bid just last week and in the low 50's area in early June," said one trader.
In June, the company reported losses for its 2nd quarter of $0.37 versus a profit of $0.11 per share.
Elsewhere, prices ended the trading day unchanged to up 1/8 with supermarkets outperforming other issues, traders said.
Grand Union 12 percent debt was bid one point higher at 71-5/8 bid, 71-7/8 offer, traders said.
Quality Food and Smith Food & Drug debt also gained 1/2 point, they said.
Ralphs Grocery 10.45's were 108-3/8 bid, 100-7/8 offer, up up 3/8, traders said.
Among steel issues, Algoma Steel traded up to 3/4 to 12-1/8, players said.
(( -- Nancy Leinfuss, 212-859-1675 ))
